## Rough Draft Oaks Project Analysis

This will be analyzing SPAD index and soil VWC (Volumetric Water Content) measurements collected at Limestone Canyon, to understand the microhabitat conditions that may affect Coast Live Oak growth. Our ANOVA analysis will first examine where the three microhabitats change the water availability in soil. Next, the regressional analysis will examine a possible relationship between the soil's VWC with the general productivity of an oak sapling, with SPAD index used a proxy.

## Loading packages

First, we will load the packages needed for this analysis.

```{r}
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(rstatix)
```

## Summary table

Next, we will load in our data sets:

```{r}
Moist_Data_Raw <- 
  read_excel("Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
             sheet = "Soil Moisture")

SPAD_Data_Raw <- 
  read_excel("Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
             sheet = "SPAD", 
             na = "NA")

Moist_Data_Raw

head(Moist_Data_Raw)

# Natural recruits were found across all treatments, not relevant for the possible differences between microhabitats
Moist_Data_Clean <- Moist_Data_Raw |> 
  filter(Treatment != "NR")

Moist_Data_Clean$Date <- as.character(Moist_Data_Clean$Date)
head(Moist_Data_Clean)

Moist_Data_Clean <- Moist_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(VWC1_perc = as.numeric(VWC1_perc))

Moist_Data_Clean <- Moist_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(VWC2_perc = as.numeric(VWC2_perc))

Moist_Data_Clean <- Moist_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(VWC3_perc = as.numeric(VWC3_perc))

# Since three VWC measurements were usually taken, we will use the average VWC for analysis
Moist_Data_Clean <- Moist_Data_Clean |> 
  group_by(Block, Treatment, VWC1_perc, VWC2_perc, VWC3_perc)|>
  mutate(VWC_avg = mean(c(VWC1_perc, VWC2_perc, VWC3_perc), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

Moist_Data_Clean

head(Moist_Data_Clean)

Moist_Data_ANOVA <- Moist_Data_Clean |> 
  group_by(Date, Block, Treatment)|>
  summarize(VWC_true_avg = mean(VWC_avg, na.rm = TRUE))

Moist_Data_Merge <- subset(Moist_Data_ANOVA, select = -Date)

#Next, we clean our SPAD data
SPAD_Data_Raw

head(SPAD_Data_Raw)

SPAD_Data_Clean <- SPAD_Data_Raw

# Similar to the filtering of Natural Recruits, dead and Natural Recruit saplings will not be considered in this analysis
SPAD_Merge <- SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  filter(Dead_Alive != 'Dead')

# Currently don't have data available to assing a soil moisture to each Natural Recruit, since they were found in variable distance away from the other treatments
SPAD_Merge <- SPAD_Merge  |>
  filter(Treatment != 'NR')

# Multiple leaf measurements were usually taken, so the average will be used
SPAD_Merge <- SPAD_Merge |> 
  group_by(Tag_Num, Treatment, Block)|>
  summarize(Leaf_avg = mean(c(Leaf1, Leaf2, Leaf3, Leaf4, Leaf5, Leaf6), na.rm = TRUE))

SPAD_Merge

# Joining our datasets together
Regression_Data <- full_join(SPAD_Merge, Moist_Data_Merge)

#Whether it was due to saplings growing in treatments we don't have VWC data for or a lack of data of any saplings growing in a treatment, any missing holes will be removed
Regression_Data <- Regression_Data |> 
  drop_na(VWC_true_avg)

# edit this later
#Regression_Data <- Regression_Data |> 
  #drop_na(Tag_Num)

Regression_Data
```

## ANOVA

We will first run a one-way ANOVA between the average VWC of the soil at each of our recorded treatments.

ggplot(Moist_Data_ANOVA) +

aes(x = Treatment, y = VWC_true_avg) +

facet_wrap(vars(Date)) +

geom_boxplot()

model \<- lm(VWC_true_avg \~ Treatment \* Date + Block , data = Moist_Data_ANOVA)

plot(model)

```{r}
# We start by looking at how our data looks

#Separate the data by date

ggplot(Moist_Data_ANOVA) +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = VWC_true_avg) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Date)) + 
  geom_boxplot()

model <- lm(VWC_true_avg ~ Treatment * Date + Block , data = Moist_Data_ANOVA)

plot(model)

# Checking normality
plot(model, which = 2)
shapiro_test(residuals(model))
# Normality is maintained

# Checking equal variance
hov <- aov(VWC_true_avg ~ Treatment + Block + Date, data = Moist_Data_ANOVA)
plot(hov, 1)   
# A large dip in our plot requires transformation

# Square root transformation creates a better Residuals vs Fitted and Q-Q Residuals plot
sqrt_hov <- aov(sqrt(VWC_true_avg) ~ Treatment * Date + Block, data = Moist_Data_ANOVA)
plot(sqrt_hov, which = 1)
plot(sqrt_hov, which = 2)

# Checking normality of residuals for the new transformed data
shapiro_test(residuals(sqrt_hov))

#Checking homoegentity of variance
car::leveneTest(log(VWC_true_avg + 1) ~ Treatment, data = Moist_Data_Merge)

# Creating One-Way Anova
model_vwc_lm <- lm(sqrt(VWC_true_avg) ~ Block + Treatment, Moist_Data_ANOVA)
anova(model_vwc_lm)
car::Anova(model_vwc_lm, type = "II")

# Due to the results of this Type II table, the treatment has no detectable effect on the VWC of soil. Since Block seems to have a statistically significant impact on VWC, there is some variable not accounted for here that is more important to predicting VWC than Treatment.

```

## Regression

Next, we will be running a regression analysis between the average VWC of soil and the average SPAD index of each oak sapling from multiple leaf measurements.

```{r}
hist(Regression_Data$VWC_true_avg)
hist(Regression_Data$Leaf_avg)

ggplot(Regression_Data) +
  geom_point() +
  aes(x = VWC_true_avg, y = Leaf_avg) + 
  theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

leaf.lm <- lm(Leaf_avg ~ VWC_true_avg, data = Regression_Data)

summary(leaf.lm)
plot(leaf.lm)

# Since all assumptions are generally met, there is a significant negative relationship between VWC and the SPAD index of an oak sapling's leaves. This means that, overall, there is likely stress and less productivity in an oak sapling growing in soil with higher VWC.

```
